issues.legal_issue: A real-estate enterprise that systematically provides services to tenants through employed workers carries on an industry.
material_facts: The company let out premises and also provided tenants with services including electricity and water, cleaning, lift operation, and electrical and sanitary repairs.
The company employed workers to provide those services, which formed part of what tenants received in return for their payments.
The enterprise conducted these activities systematically.
issues.conclusion: The company’s activity fell within the meaning of “industry” in Section 2(j) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(j) is applied according to the functional test stated in Bangalore Water Supply & Sewerage Board v. R. Rajappa, which restored the broad approach in D.N. Banerjee v. P.R. Mukherjee, Corporation of the City of Nagpur v. Its Employees, and State of Bombay v. Hospital Mazdoor Sabha. Systematic activity involving cooperation between employer and employees to provide material services is prima facie an industry; the profit motive is irrelevant. Management of Safdar Jung Hospital v. Kuldip Singh Sethi was overruled by Bangalore Water Supply.

predicates.labor_dispute_industry_classification: The case requires deciding whether an enterprise’s activity is an industry for purposes of a labor dispute.
predicates.systematic_tenant_services: The enterprise systematically provides material services to people who occupy its premises, and those services form part of what they receive for their payments.
predicates.employed_workers_provide_services: The enterprise employs workers to provide those services.

issues.definition: When a labor-dispute industry classification concerns an enterprise that systematically provides material services through its employed workers, the enterprise’s activity is an industry.

issues.legal_issue: A settlement may be terminated by notice inferred from correspondence that clearly communicates an intention to terminate it, without a formal notice document.
material_facts: An earlier award was in force when the union sent a letter communicating the employees’ intention to terminate it.
The letter was sent to the employer, which acknowledged awareness of the union’s intention in later correspondence.
The reference was made after the applicable interval had elapsed.
issues.conclusion: The earlier award had been validly terminated, and a formal notice of termination was not required.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(b), 2(p), 19(2), and 19(6) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 govern awards, settlements, and their termination. Under Indian Link Chain Manufacturers Ltd. v. Their Workmen, notice of termination can be inferred from correspondence; Section 19(2) does not require a formal notice. The clear communication of the intention to terminate and the elapsed interval supported the finding that the prior award had been terminated.

predicates.industrial_dispute_reference_after_prior: A labor dispute is referred for adjudication while an earlier award is asserted to remain in force.
predicates.correspondence_communicates_termination_: Correspondence clearly communicates a party’s intention to terminate the earlier award or settlement.
predicates.employer_receives_communication: The employer receives the communication or otherwise becomes aware of the intention to terminate.
predicates.required_termination_interval_elapsed: The applicable interval after notice has elapsed before the new reference is made.

issues.definition: If a labor dispute is referred while a prior award is asserted to remain in force, but correspondence clearly communicates termination intent, reaches the employer, and the required interval elapses, the prior award is validly terminated.

issues.legal_issue: A plea raised for the first time in an appeal to the Supreme Court that requires an inquiry into facts cannot be raised at that stage.
material_facts: The employer first raised the objection that the requirements for a notice to terminate an award had not been met in the Supreme Court.
Deciding that objection required an inquiry into facts.
issues.conclusion: The objection could not be agitated for the first time in the Supreme Court.
issues.legal_principle: On an appeal under Article 133(1)(a) of the Constitution, a question first raised in the Supreme Court that involves an inquiry into questions of fact cannot be allowed to be agitated.

predicates.appeal_to_supreme_court: The matter is an appeal before the Supreme Court.
predicates.factual_plea_raised_for_first_time: A party raises the plea for the first time in that appeal.
predicates.resolving_plea_requires_fact_inquiry: Determining the plea requires an inquiry into facts.

issues.definition: In an appeal to the Supreme Court, a plea raised for the first time that requires an inquiry into facts is not considered.

issues.legal_issue: In judicial review of an industrial tribunal’s findings, a party generally cannot rely on material that was not before the tribunal when the party gives no justification for failing to produce it there.
material_facts: The employer sought reconsideration of the tribunal’s award based on documents submitted during the High Court proceedings that had not been before the tribunal.
The employer did not show why those documents had not been produced before the tribunal or that it had been prevented from producing them.
The High Court was reviewing the tribunal’s findings under Article 226 of the Constitution.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was right to generally consider the material before the tribunal and to refuse reconsideration based on the later-submitted documents when no justification for their earlier omission was shown.
issues.legal_principle: In exercising jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution to review an industrial tribunal’s findings, a High Court should generally consider the material that was before the tribunal and should not normally admit fresh or further material. Where the party does not explain why the material was not produced before the tribunal, there is no justification for reconsidering the award on that basis.

predicates.article_226_review_of_tribunal_findings: A court is reviewing an industrial tribunal’s findings under constitutional judicial-review jurisdiction.
predicates.party_relies_on_material_not_before_trib: A party relies on material in the reviewing court that was not before the tribunal.
predicates.no_reason_given_for_omission: The party does not explain why the material was not produced before the tribunal or show that it was prevented from doing so.

issues.definition: In judicial review of tribunal findings, when a party relies on material not before the tribunal and gives no reason for its omission, reconsideration based on that material is refused.
